title: Magnetic Properties of High-Entropy Alloy FeCoNiTi

recollection.starting_material: Guess: Elemental powders or precursors of Fe, Co, Ni, and Ti were used to fabricate the alloy.
recollection.intervention: Guess: The alloy was synthesized via a high-temperature technique (such as arc melting or induction melting) followed by homogenization or heat-treatment to obtain a uniform high-entropy alloy.
recollection.structure: Guess: The resulting structure was a single-phase solid solution with either an FCC or BCC (or mixed) crystal structure characteristic of high-entropy alloys.
recollection.mechanism: Guess: The magnetic properties were attributed to the complex interplay between the disordered atomic lattice and the magnetic interactions of the Fe, Co, and Ni elements, with Ti possibly influencing lattice distortion and electron scattering. This disorder is thought to enhance magnetic exchange interactions or modify anisotropy.
recollection.results: Guess: The paper likely reported enhanced saturation magnetization and controlled coercivity relative to conventional alloys. For example, quantitative measurements might include a saturation magnetization in the range of 100–150 emu/g and a coercivity of a few tens to hundreds of Oe, though the exact numbers are not remembered.

score.note: The recollection generically suggests arc melting, but misses rapid quenching and the compositionally matched C14-dominant comparison alloy. It incorrectly characterizes the material as a generic single-phase FCC/BCC solid solution rather than an fcc+C14 Laves dual-phase alloy with chemical segregation. The magnetic explanation is nonspecific and omits antiferromagnetic sublattice coupling, orbital-moment/domain-wall pinning, and phase-specific transitions. The guessed magnetization and coercivity ranges do not recover the reported 667 Oe at 400 K or the 1084, 214, and 168 K transitions.
